prime.problem: Every step of an agent is one tool call, and most agent bugs live in its three pieces: a vague tool description, a result sent back in the wrong shape (a 400 error), or a result so long or so unclear that the model loses the thread. Seeing the real JSON makes all three concrete.
prime.fits: Zooms into one turn of the agent loop. What the tool sends back becomes part of every later call, which is the bridge to the next card on what the model sees.
prime.goal: Write a correct tool definition and reply message for two parallel calls, and compute what cutting a long tool output saves over the rest of a run.

attend: Which field ties a tool_result back to the call it answers?
What two formatting mistakes turn the next request into a 400 error?
Why did showing the whole file score worse than a 100-line window in SWE-agent?
Where do the 32,500 and 10,125 tokens in the log example come from?
What must the truncation note say so that cutting doesn't hide the key line?

must: The model can't run code → it writes a tool_use block with an id, name and input → the harness runs it and answers with a tool_result carrying the same tool_use_id
Parallel calls arrive in one response → every id must be answered in the very next user message, results before any text → otherwise the next request fails with a 400
A tool that fails still answers → is_error: true plus what went wrong and what to try next → the model recovers instead of guessing or the loop crashing
Every tool result is re-sent on every later call → a 26,000-character log costs 6,500 tokens per call, 2,025 if cut to head and tail → cap output at the tool and say what was cut
elevated: More output is not more help → SWE-agent's whole-file view (12.7%) and one-match-at-a-time search (12.0%) scored below the bounded versions (18.0%) → tool defaults are design choices to measure
reference: mini-swe-agent's 10,000/5,000-character cut and Claude Code's 30,000-character bash cap

compress.prompt: From memory, write the three JSON pieces for one run_tests call (definition, tool_use, tool_result), then add a second parallel call that fails and show the reply message. Finish with the token arithmetic for the cut vs uncut log.
checklist: definition: name, description, input_schema (type object, properties, required)
response: tool_use blocks with id, name, input; stop_reason tool_use
reply: one user message, a tool_result per id, results before text, is_error on the failure
errors say what to do next, and truncation says what was cut and how to see it

retrieve.q: Name the three parts of a tool definition and say which one the model reads to decide whether and how to call the tool.
answer: the description tells the model when and why to use it
the input_schema lists the allowed arguments; the model's input must fit it

retrieve.q: The model asks for run_tests and view in one response, and view raises an exception. Describe the exact message your harness sends back.
answer: one user message with two tool_result blocks, one per tool_use_id
the tool_result blocks come before any text
view's result has is_error: true and a message naming the problem and a next step, like the likely correct path

retrieve.q: Your tool can return the full 26,000-character log or its first and last 4,000 characters. Argue for one, naming what each costs.
answer: full: 6,500 tokens on every later call, and the key lines are harder to find
cut: 2,025 tokens, but the middle is hidden, so the note must say what was cut and how to see it
cut is usually right because pytest's summary is at the end, but not when the one line that matters is in the middle

compare.q: The agent-loop card added 1,500 tokens per tool result. What happens to that run's total if one result is instead the uncut 6,500-token log at call 2?
answer: the extra 5,000 tokens join the history from call 3 on
calls 3–6 each carry them: 4 × 5,000 = 20,000 more input tokens
that is 37% more than the 54,000-token total, from one tool call

compare.q: Context growth assumed a steady 2,000 tokens per turn. How does one oversized tool result change the shape of its bars, and how would you spot it in a log?
answer: a single step up in input tokens right after that call
every later bar stays higher by the same amount
plot input tokens per call: a jump after one tool call is the signature

predict.q: SWE-agent's search tool had three versions: a summary capped at 50 matches, no search tool at all, and one match at a time. Before looking, rank them by bugs fixed.
predict.answer: Summary 18.0%, no search 15.7%, one-at-a-time 12.0%. The one-at-a-time version did worse than having no search tool, because the agent paged through matches until its budget ran out. A badly designed tool can be worse than no tool.

apply.task: Pick one tool in an agent you use or are building (a test runner, a file viewer, a search). Run it on a case that produces long output and on a case that fails. Write down what the model would receive in each case, its size in tokens (characters ÷ 4), and rewrite the error message so it names the next action.
apply.done: You have the token size of the long output, a head-and-tail version with a note of what was cut, and an error message a model could act on without re-reading anything.
apply.hint: Good error text answers two questions: what went wrong, and what should the next call be?
